changes.after: typedef gives a type a shorter name. A struct can link to another struct through a pointer.

before: typedef gives an existing type another name. typedef struct Node Node allows Node where you would otherwise write struct Node. It does not allocate a node.

Within the structure definition, struct Node *next refers to a node without embedding a whole node. A structure cannot directly contain a full instance of itself: that would require an unbounded size. NULL can mark the end of this short chain.

Expected output or behavior: 8

after: An alias is another name for the same thing. typedef creates a type alias. `typedef struct Node Node;` lets you write Node instead of struct Node. It creates a name, not a stored node.

A node is one item in a linked group. This Node stores a value and a pointer named next. A pointer can refer to another Node without storing that whole Node inside itself. NULL marks the end of this short chain.
start.next points to end. `start.next->value` follows that pointer and reads end's value, so it prints 8. Both nodes are still alive at that point.
Change end's starting value to 12. The link still leads to the same node, so it reads that node's new starting value.
